On paper, it looks like Sebastien Pocognoli has opted for a five-back formation, with Swansea City defender Stephen Welsh making his Scotland debut as one of the centre backs.

Captain Andy Robertson and Brentford’s Aaron Hickey will operate as the wing-backs, with Billy Gilmour, Lewis Ferguson and John McGinn forming a midfield three.

A new-look attack is spearheaded by the returning Oli McBurnie and 22-year-old Robbie Ure, who like Welsh, will also make his Scotland debut.

Angus Gunn remains his country’s first-choice goalkeeper.

Sebastien Pocognoli's first Scotland XI to take on Slovenia 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁳󠁣󠁴󠁿Watch the game live on BBC One Scotland from 13:45 BST 📺#BBCFootball pic.twitter.com/OnfWR7Gp8C

Debutants Robbie Ure and Stephen Welsh are each poised for their first international cap. Billy Gilmour returns to the starting XI after missing the World Cup through injury and Oli McBurnie will make his first appearance for Scotland since 2021.

Sébastien Pocognoli's first Scotland starting XI 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁳󠁣󠁴󠁿#SVNSCO pic.twitter.com/JC6RGOq1QJ

“The first game is always a special game so you have to bring the mental aspect in for the players and for the staff.

“A good result can help but the most important thing is we see things that we work on through the week. I hope is we apply that well then we will get the result which will be the perfect mix.

“I hope we can bring a good game, and a good exciting principle on the pitch. I think we need the support from the supporters because there’s a lot of new players.

“We need to create a good energy but it’s up to us on the pitch to create this. So then we can be hand in hand with the supporters.”

Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of this UEFA Nations League B, Group 1 match as Slovenia host Scotland at Stozice Stadium in Ljubljana.

Scotland qualified for their first World Cup in 28 years this summer, but they exited the tournament with a whimper after failing to finish as one of the best third-place group sides. Steve Clarke’s men beat tournament debutants Haiti 1-0 in their opening match, before falling to defeats without scoring against Morocco and Brazil.

Following the World Cup, Clarke stepped down as Scotland’s head coach, ending a seven-year tenure, and was replaced by Belgian manager Sebastien Pocognoli. The former Monaco boss will take charge of his first game in his new role today and will be itching to make an encouraging start in a new era for Scottish football.

Over this extended international break, Pocognoli’s side will also face Switzerland and North Macedonia, as well as a return fixture against Slovenia in Scotland on October 6 to round off a busy period.

While Scotland took part in the World Cup, Slovenia were reflecting on their hugely disappointing qualification performance, where they finished third in their group behind Switzerland and Kosovo without winning and netting just three goals across six matches.

Manchester United striker Benjamin Sesko – Slovenia’s star man and most well-known player – withdrew from Bostjan Cesar’s squad earlier this week after the recurrence of a shin injury caused the 23-year-old to completely miss the 1-1 draw against Fulham last Sunday.

Scotland have a few notable absences, with Scott McTominay, Che Adams and Lawrence Shankland all unavailable, but Billy Gilmour returns to the fold after missing the World Cup through injury, Oli McBurnie has been recalled and Sevilla striker Robbie Ure has received his first senior call-up.

Kick-off is at 14:00, with team news coming shortly.

Arsenal have been warned not to make a rushed decision over Viktor Gyokeres when the January transfer window opens.

The Sweden international has endured a difficult season, with Kai Havertz currently ahead of him in Mikel Arteta’s preferred starting XI. That has inevitably fuelled speculation over a possible winter exit, especially with some pundits questioning whether Gyokeres is the right fit for Arsenal’s system.

However, former Gunners striker Jeremie Aliadiere believes selling him midway through the season could create an even bigger problem.

Speaking to Metro, Aliadiere argued that Arsenal must think carefully before sanctioning Gyokeres’ departure.

“I think it’s all depending on the finances how much they can get for him and who to replace him with,” he said.

His main concern is squad depth. Havertz may be first choice, but Arsenal would leave themselves dangerously short if Gyokeres departed without a replacement already secured.

“If Havertz gets injured, which obviously we’ve seen in the past – he’s had a few injuries and he can pick up injuries – you just end up with no striker at all,” Aliadiere added.

That warning comes amid growing debate over Gyokeres’ future. CaughtOffside reported in October that Micah Richards believes Arsenal should consider moving him on if his form does not improve.

There is a fair argument that Gyokeres has not fully adapted to Arteta’s preferred style. Sky Sports recently highlighted how Havertz offers more in possession, combination play and pressing, which helps explain why he has become the favoured option.

But that does not automatically mean Arsenal should sell.

Gyokeres still offers something different. His power, direct running and ability to attack space can be useful in games where Arsenal need a more traditional No.9. The striker has grown frustrated with his limited Premier League starts and could consider leaving.

From Arsenal’s perspective, the smartest approach would be to keep him unless a clear upgrade is ready to arrive.

Selling first and searching for a replacement later would be an unnecessary gamble. Arsenal are competing on multiple fronts, and one injury to Havertz could quickly make Gyokeres far more important than he currently appears.

A world record 51 red cards were shown in one game during an Under-20 match in Brazil following a mass brawl.

The Guinness Book of World Records has confirmed that the game saw the most dismissals ever, with 43 players and eight members of coaching staff given their marching orders.

Said record came after the Minas Gerais Under-20 Championship clash between Uberlandia and Mamore descended into chaos following an altercation near the technical areas.

Uberlandia had initially been reduced to ten men after Luike Bispo dos Santos struck an opposing player in the stomach.

In the 54th minute of the game, nearly four football teams' worth of players were involved in an incident that saw some players chasing others, with military police called to the stadium.

The referee reported that six ball boys were also involved, and threw punches, kicks and objects at players and coaching staff.

A record 51 players were shown a red card amid a mass brawl during a Brazilian match

Weapons were also said to have been used, including stretchers and chairs. The chaos took well over half an hour to cool.

#1373. Spalletti: ‘When Juventus win, people act like opponents are weak or ridiculous’

Luciano Spalletti took the opportunity to stand up for Juventus after a 2-1 Europa League victory at AZ Alkmaar. ‘When we win, people act like our opponents are weak or ridiculous, but we showed courage.’

It was far from an easy task for the Bianconeri, as AZ Alkmaar were unbeaten at home in 17 European fixtures going back to October 2023, and the Old Lady was decimated by injuries.

They surged into a 2-0 lead with Randal Kolo Muani providing the assist for Teun Koopmeiners, facing his hometown club, and then the ex-PSG striker scored the second himself when combining with Nick Woltemade.

It was a very tense finale, as AZ Alkmaar fought back with the Mexx Meerdink tap-in after Lloyd Kelly was robbed on the touchline, then Juve rode their luck as Meerdink was offside for a potential equaliser in added time.

“I am very satisfied, because we played well against a very strong team,” Spalletti told Sky Sport Italia.

“I remember when all of you laughed in my face when we beat NEC 5-0, you acted as if they were a ridiculous team, but NEC now have seven points in the Europa League.

“So perhaps people need to re-evaluate how they consider us, humility, and giving credit to a team without just constantly wanting to put pressure on.

“When we win a game, people act as if it was because the opponents were weak, or finding some excuses. We played a strong game against a great team tonight, and as we saw the moment our intensity dropped, they will take advantage.

“We’ve seen in the Champions League, Europa League, these sides might have a predictable way of doing things, but it becomes a strength when they can do it that many times. It is constantly hammering away at those situations, we were pinned back, worried about whether or not to push out from defence, and a through ball caused a goal.

“There were mad scrambles, if the game lasted for another three or four minutes, I don’t think we would’ve taken the result home.”

Considering Juventus were so in control for 70-odd minutes, Spalletti sees the need for insurance rather than learning how to defend a lead better.

“What we needed to do was score a third goal. The way we played, we had to score a third goal there. When you win away to a team that hasn’t lost at home in 17 European games, winning 14 of them, that is a sign you played with authority and quality. We showed the right courage.”

Koopmeiners and Kolo Muani had arguably their best performances of the season so far in the Juventus jersey, yet Spalletti wanted more.

“Kolo had a few situations when he had the chance to get running and become unstoppable, but we never managed to give him the right pass to get into that space. So we had to suffer on the edge of the area, we did it well too.

“Those who came off the bench could really do damage on the counter with Boga and Ekhator, instead we got pinned back and felt anxious, nobody was sure whether to come or go, and got stuck in the middle.”

This performance does build on Sunday’s 2-0 Serie A victory against Napoli and suggest Juventus might be on the right track, while they are certainly flying high in the Europa League with three wins and a 2-2 draw against Rennes.

“Some like Lucumi did the unseen dirty work, he often had to deal with the ball on his right foot, it was not his position and he did it well. Kalulu plays almost non-stop, the poor thing was about to ask for a substitution at the end as he was exhausted.

“There were many positive signs today, but the most important was that we went into their half, accepted being man to man for a long time.”

Spalletti was impressed by AZ Alkmaar goalkeeper Jari De Busser and feels Italian teams can learn from this Dutch approach.

“In Italy so many said a goalkeeper just has to make saves, but when he can play with his feet like this, he annuls all the pressing that the opponents do, he neutralises any situation that you prepare, and he is the extra man. The goalkeeper makes the difference. Did you see the pass he made to spark that move?

“The fact we came here and accepted that duel, pushing into their half and accepting the challenge, was the biggest victory. I also liked the attitude from those on the bench, who shouted and experienced it as if they were on the field.”

Now Juventus must prepare for their final match before the break for international duty, a tricky Serie A trip to old rivals Fiorentina on Sunday evening.

“My concern is the way we conceded the goal, with everyone waiting to see who would take it, allowing the others to move around. I continue to say a decision that is not made is the worst possible kind, even more so than a bad decision.

“Being hesitant, waiting for the situation to develop, that is what I do not want to see.”
